title: Foundations for Causal Inference
text:
These are the in-depth lecture notes for our course Foundations for Causal Inference.
The objective of the course is to build, step by step, the foundations necessary for a rigorous understanding of causal inference, connecting theory with real-world applications.

Access to this content is restricted to enrolled students. All material is privately owned, protected, and traceable. Its use is strictly limited to enrolled students for the duration of the course.

The main learning path will cover:

Probability
Statistical Inference
Regression
Causal Inference

These in-depth lecture notes serve as supplementary material for learning, study, and reference.

title: What Do We Want to Learn from Data?
section: 1. Description: what happened in the data we observed?
text:
1. Description: what happened in the data we observed?

The question
Sometimes we simply want to summarize what we have already observed.
For example:

What was the churn rate last quarter?
How many users converted in this campaign?
What was the average revenue per customer?
Which segment had the highest conversion?
How many orders were delivered late?

If we had 10,000 customers in the quarter and 1,000 churned, then the observed churn rate was 10%.
That number describes those data. We do not need Statistical Inference to say that.
The important point is to distinguish between:

describing what happened in the observed data

and

using those data to learn something that goes beyond them.

That second question is precisely where Statistical Inference begins.


Why does a company want to describe the data?
Because before predicting, inferring, or estimating causal effects, we need to understand what happened.
Description appears in virtually all data work:

dashboards;
KPIs;
reports;
product monitoring;
revenue tracking;
funnel analysis;
comparisons across periods and segments.







Main idea



Description answers what happened in the data we observed. By itself, it does not require generalizing to a population, predicting new observations, or interpreting relationships as causal.
crumbs: 2  What Do We Want to Learn from Data?

title: What Do We Want to Learn from Data?
section: 2. Prediction: what is likely to happen?
text:
2. Prediction: what is likely to happen?

The question
In predictive problems, we want to anticipate an outcome that is still unknown.
For example:

Will this customer churn?
Is this transaction fraud?
Is this user likely to buy?
How much will we sell next month?
How long will this delivery take?
Which lead is likely to convert?
Which product should we recommend to this user?

The goal is to learn, from the observed data, a function \(f\) capable of transforming the available information (\(X\)) into a good prediction of \(Y\) for new cases.
A general way to represent this relationship is:
\[
Y = f(X) + \epsilon
\]
When the goal is prediction, the main thing is that the learned function should produce good predictions and generalize to new data.
That is:

when new observations of \(X\) arrive, will we be able to predict their corresponding values of \(Y\) well through the learned rule \(f\)?



Why does a company want to predict something?
Because anticipating an event allows it to act before the event occurs.

predict churn → prioritize customers for retention;
predict fraud → block or review transactions;
predict demand → organize inventory and operations;
predict conversion → prioritize leads;
predict interest → personalize recommendations.

Prediction usually takes us into the domain of Statistical Learning and Machine Learning.
Among its main foundations are:

Probability Theory;
linear algebra;
calculus and optimization;
loss functions;
train, validation, and test;
generalization;
overfitting and regularization;
cross-validation;
performance metrics;
Machine Learning algorithms.

In a purely predictive problem, the main goal is not to estimate a population quantity and quantify its uncertainty, but to build a function that generalizes well to new data.
For this reason, Statistical Inference is in general not a prerequisite for building a good predictive model.
But it may appear later, when we change the question. It can also appear within a predictive problem, as a necessary layer in evaluating what was done.
Suppose two churn models have AUCs of 0.81 and 0.83 on the same test sample.
If we ask:

Which model had better observed performance?

we are simply comparing observed results.
But if we ask:

Is this difference of 0.02 likely to persist for new cases, or could it simply be the result of the sample we used?

we enter a problem of Statistical Inference.
Further below, you will understand that this question contains something very important implicitly:

To know what happens in new cases, it would be useful to know more about the “Process of Nature that Generated the Data.”

However, since it is usually not possible to have that knowledge in the real world, we use a sample to infer something about that Data-Generating Process.






Main idea



Prediction creates value when correctly anticipating an event allows the company to act better before it occurs.

title: What Do We Want to Learn from Data?
section: 3. Statistical Inference: what can we learn beyond the observed data?
text:
3. Statistical Inference: what can we learn beyond the observed data?

The question
Now the question changes.
We no longer want only to describe the data we have already seen, nor necessarily to predict the outcome of a new individual observation.
We want to use the observed data to learn some unknown quantity about a population or about the process that generates the data.
Why is this necessary?
Imagine someone asks:

What is the true churn rate of our customers?

That quantity belongs to the data-generating process — the data-generating process (DGP).
If we knew that process completely, we would know exactly with what probabilities different outcomes are generated, and we could calculate directly the churn rate we care about.
We would not need to estimate it from the observed data.
In practice, however, we do not know the DGP.
What we observe is only one realization of that process: a sample of customers, transactions, users, or events.
It is from that sample that we try to learn some unknown characteristic of the larger process that generated the data.
That is exactly where Statistical Inference comes in:

use the observed data to learn about an unknown quantity of the population or of the data-generating process, and quantify the uncertainty of that conclusion.

For example:

Does the observed churn rate represent the churn level of our customers well?
Is the average conversion observed in this period a good approximation of what we should expect more generally?
Does the difference in conversion between two groups seem real, or could it simply be data variation?
Did churn really increase, or are we observing a fluctuation compatible with the variability of the process?

Here is the essential distinction:

If we only calculate a metric on the observed data, we are describing those data.

Statistical Inference begins when we want to use that metric to say something beyond the observed sample.


An example with churn
Suppose we had 10,000 customers this quarter and 1,000 churned.
The observed rate was:

10%

If the question is:

What was the churn rate of those 10,000 customers?

then the problem is over: 10%. That is Descriptive Statistics.
But the company may want to use that number for planning, targets, or future decisions.
The question then becomes something like:

Does this churn of 10% represent well the churn level we should expect from our customers more generally?

Now uncertainty exists.
Another sample of customers, another period, or another realization of the same process could produce 9%, 11%, 13%, or some other value.
The observed 10% then starts being used as an estimate of a quantity we do not observe directly: the underlying churn level of the population or of the process that generates these customers.
This is when concepts such as:

estimator;
sampling distribution;
standard error;
confidence interval;
hypothesis tests.

come in.
An intuitive way to think about this is:

the customers who have already churned belong to the past. To know what happened to them, we just need to look at the data. Statistical Inference appears when we use those customers to learn something we want to transport beyond them — including to customers and periods we have not yet observed.



Why does a company want to do inference?
Because metrics vary, but not every observed variation means the business truly changed.
Conversion changes from one week to another. Churn changes from one month to another. Average revenue changes across samples. Segments show different results.
Part of this variation may simply be a consequence of the uncertainty inherent in the data-generating process. Even if nothing relevant changed in the business, different samples produced by the same process will not be exactly identical.
Consider a simple example: rolling a die and observing the result. If we completely knew the data-generating process, we would know the probability of each outcome. Even so, we would not know in advance which number will appear on a particular roll.
This is the uncertainty inherent in the process: even knowing its probabilities perfectly, different realizations can produce different results. We might observe 1, then 3, then 1 again, without anything having changed in the die or in the process that generates it.
But knowing those probabilities would give us something fundamental: we would know what variation is normal and expected for that process, and we could make decisions based on that structure.
In companies (or in the real world more generally), the problem is that we usually do not know the generating process nor its probabilities. We only have the data it produced, and we try to learn about the process from them using statistical inference.
So observing that conversion dropped from 10% to 9.7% is not enough to conclude that a real change occurred. Perhaps something changed. But perhaps the same process, working exactly as before, could naturally produce 10% in one sample and 9.7% in another.
An important function of Statistical Inference is precisely to quantify this uncertainty and help separate:

a difference that suggests a change in the data-generating process

from

a difference still compatible with the variability that the process itself can generate.

If we treat every observed variation as a real business change (that is, as something inherent to the business data-generating process), we may react to noise.
This distinction helps avoid hasty decisions and better understand what the data really allow us to conclude.


What do we need to learn in order to do Statistical Inference?
Probability Theory provides the mathematical language to represent uncertainty and reason about what could happen if we repeated the process of generating and sampling the data.
Then come concepts such as:

sampling;
statistics and estimators;
sampling distributions;
Law of Large Numbers;
Central Limit Theorem;
standard error;
estimation;
properties of estimators;
confidence intervals;
hypothesis tests;
p-values;
Type I and Type II errors.

This construction makes it possible to transform:

“we observed this number”

into something like:

“based on the data and on the assumptions of our model, this is our best estimate of the quantity of interest, and this is the uncertainty associated with it.”







Main idea



Description says what happened in the data we observed. Statistical Inference uses the data we observed to learn about what we do not fully observe, quantifying the uncertainty of that step.

text:
The same churn problem, four different questions
Now we can return to the same example and clearly separate the four types of question:








Company question
What do we want to learn?
Type of problem




“What was our churn last quarter?”
What happened to the observed customers.
Description


“Which customers are likely to churn?”
The likely outcome for new cases.
Prediction


“We observed 10% churn. Does this number represent the churn level of our customers well, or could it vary substantially?”
A quantity that goes beyond the observed sample, and the uncertainty associated with it.
Statistical Inference


“If we offer a benefit, will churn decrease? By how much?”
The effect of an intervention.
Causal Inference



The difference can be summarized like this:

Description: what happened?
Prediction: what is likely to happen?
Statistical Inference: what can we learn beyond the data we observed, and with what uncertainty?
Causal Inference: what would happen if we changed something?

title: What Do We Want to Learn from Data?
text:
A mental map
When you face a new Data Science problem, start with these questions:

Do I only want to summarize what happened?

What happened in the data we observed?

Description



Do I want to anticipate an outcome?

What is likely to happen?

Prediction



Do I want to learn something beyond the observed data and quantify uncertainty?

What do the data allow me to conclude beyond the sample?

Statistical Inference



Do I want to know the effect of changing something?

What would happen if I intervened?

Causal Inference

And only afterwards ask:

Which method or model should I use?

title: What Do We Want to Learn from Data?
section: The model does not define the question
text:
The model does not define the question
It is important not to automatically associate certain algorithms with certain paradigms.
For example:

regression = Statistical Inference

or

XGBoost = Prediction.

A regression can be used for Prediction, Statistical Inference, or within a causal analysis.
Machine Learning can also be used within Causal Inference.
Therefore:

the algorithm does not define the problem. The question defines the problem.

The model is a tool chosen only after we know what we want to learn.

title: What Do We Want to Learn from Data?
section: And where does Bayesian Statistics fit in?
text:
And where does Bayesian Statistics fit in?
Bayesian Statistics is not a fifth category parallel to the four above.
It offers another way to represent and update uncertainty from data.
Bayesian methods can be used in:

Prediction;
Statistical Inference;
Causal Inference;
decision making.

For now, it is enough to keep in mind that:

“Bayesian” and “Frequentist” refer to frameworks of inference, and do not replace the distinction between describing, predicting, inferring, and estimating causal effects.

We will return to these ideas later. However, we will not cover Bayesian Statistics in this course.

text:
Where does this course fit in?
This course is not a predictive Machine Learning course.
Our path will be aimed mainly at:

Statistical Inference and Causal Inference.

To get there, we will build the necessary foundations:
Mathematics
↓
Probability Theory
↓
Statistical Inference
↓
Regression
↓
Causal Inference
We will begin with Mathematics and Probability Theory, because we need a rigorous language to represent uncertainty.
Then we will study Statistical Inference, learning how observed data can be used to learn about quantities that go beyond the sample, and how to quantify the uncertainty of those conclusions.
We will study Regression, one of the most important tools for modeling relationships between variables and a fundamental bridge to Causal Inference.
Finally, we will arrive at Causal Inference, where we will add a new question:

What would happen if we intervened in the world?

title: What Do We Want to Learn from Data?
text:
What to remember
Before choosing any model, ask:

What do we want to learn from the data?

Description
What happened in the data we observed?
→ Helps the company understand and measure what happened.
Prediction
What is likely to happen?
→ Helps the company anticipate.
Statistical Inference
What can we learn beyond the observed data, and with what uncertainty?
→ Helps the company generalize without treating an observed metric as the exact truth about the whole.
Causal Inference
What would happen if we did something?
→ Helps the company discover which actions truly change outcomes.
Models come afterwards. The question comes first.

title: The Map of Probability and Inference
text:
1. Probability Theory: why do we build probabilistic models?
Before we begin, I want to make clear where we are going.
The central idea of this course is simple and can be seen through two distinct but deeply connected movements:
When some characteristic of this mechanism is unknown — such as a mean, a conversion probability, or some other quantity of interest — we use the observed data to learn about it.
It is from this relationship between model and data that the two major ideas we will connect throughout the course arise: Probability and Statistical Inference.
In the real world there are phenomena whose individual outcome we cannot determine in advance with certainty.
There is uncertainty at the individual level, that is, if you carry out one trial of an experiment, you do not know what may happen.
But uncertainty does not mean a complete absence of structure.
And having some structure is very important, because that is where mathematics comes in to understand and model the phenomenon.
Notice something interesting. When we observe many occurrences of certain phenomena, aggregate regularities may appear: some outcomes occur more often than others, some proportions seem to stabilize, and certain patterns reappear in the data.
This combination of individual uncertainty with aggregate regularity is a useful way to think about what we call chance regularity (chance and regularity).
\[
\begin{array}{c}
\boxed{\text{uncertain real phenomenon}} \\
\Downarrow \\
\boxed{\text{unpredictable individual outcomes}} \\
\Downarrow \\
\boxed{\text{regularities may appear in the aggregate}}
\end{array}
\]
Probability Theory provides a mathematical language to represent this kind of phenomenon.
Instead of trying to describe each individual outcome in advance, we build a mathematical representation of the uncertain mechanism that could produce those outcomes.
We will call this representation a probability model.
\[
\begin{array}{c}
\boxed{\text{REAL WORLD}} \\
\Downarrow \\
\boxed{\text{uncertain phenomenon}} \\
\Downarrow \\
\boxed{\text{observable regularities}} \\
\Downarrow \\
\boxed{\text{mathematical representation}} \\
\Downarrow \\
\boxed{\text{PROBABILITY MODEL}}
\end{array}
\]
This is the first movement of our map:
\[
\begin{array}{c}
\boxed{\text{uncertain phenomenon}} \\
\Downarrow \\
\boxed{\text{mathematical representation}} \\
\Downarrow \\
\boxed{\text{probability model}} \\
\Downarrow \\
\boxed{\text{study what this model implies}}
\end{array}
\]

title: The Map of Probability and Inference
section: 2. Statistical Inference: when the model meets the data
text:
2. Statistical Inference: when the model meets the data
In practice, however, we rarely know all the characteristics of the mechanism we are trying to represent.
We may know how to represent a phenomenon probabilistically, but still not know some important quantity in the model: a mean, a variance, a conversion probability, among others.
That is where the second movement of our map appears.
Instead of starting from a fully specified model and asking only what it implies, we observe data and ask:

What do these data allow us to learn about the unknown characteristics of the probabilistic mechanism that could have produced them?

\[
\begin{array}{c}
\boxed{\text{probability model with something unknown}} \\
+ \\
\boxed{\text{observed data}} \\
\Downarrow \\
\boxed{\text{learn about the mechanism}}
\end{array}
\]
This is where Statistical Inference is born. It does not abandon Probability: it uses precisely the probabilistic structure of the model to connect what we observe to what we want to learn.
With these two movements in mind, we can compare two simple situations.
crumbs: 3  The Map of Probability and Inference

title: The Map of Probability and Inference
section: Case 1 — the model is completely specified
text:
Case 1 — the model is completely specified
Consider a coin that we decide to model as fair.
Here, we begin from the assumption that we already have a Probability Model for the world.
We define
\[
X=
\begin{cases}
1, & \text{if heads occurs},\\
0, & \text{if tails occurs}.
\end{cases}
\]
And we specify the model, that is, we assume that this phenomenon follows something like
\[
X\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(0.5).
\]
The value \(0.5\) did not appear because the axioms of Probability force a coin to have that probability.
It is part of our modeling of the coin as fair, that is,
\[
P(X=1)=P(X=0)=0.5.
\]
In this example, the physical symmetry of the coin helps justify the hypothesis of equal probabilities. In other problems, the assumptions may come from other sources.
Now imagine 100 tosses:
\[
X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_{100}.
\]
Since the model is completely specified (in the sense that we are assuming we know all the parameters, including the \(p\)), we can ask:

If I toss this coin 100 times, what is the probability of observing exactly 50 heads?

And calculate
\[
P\left(\sum_{i=1}^{100}X_i=50\right)
=
\binom{100}{50}(0.5)^{100}.
\]
The direction of reasoning is:
\[
\begin{array}{c}
\boxed{\text{we already have a specified probability model}} \\
\Downarrow \\
\boxed{\text{what does this model imply mathematically?}} \\
\Downarrow \\
\boxed{\text{we arrive at possible data and their probabilities}}
\end{array}
\]
Here we are doing Probability:

we start from a specified model and deduce its consequences.
crumbs: 3  The Map of Probability and Inference

title: The Map of Probability and Inference
section: Case 2 — part of the model is unknown
text:
Case 2 — part of the model is unknown
Now consider something much closer to the day-to-day of Data Science: checkout conversion.
For each observed user session on the website, we define
\[
X=
\begin{cases}
1, & \text{if there was a purchase},\\
0, & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
Motivated by our prior knowledge of Probability Models, we can represent this outcome by a Bernoulli:
\[
X\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p).
\]
But now there is a fundamental difference: we do not know the value of
\[
p=P(X=1),
\]
that is, the conversion probability in the model.
In this case, unfortunately there is no physical symmetry here that gives us something like \(p=0.5\) in advance and helps us arrive at a final answer.
We know one possible way to represent the phenomenon probabilistically, but one characteristic of the model remains unknown.
That is where the data come in (and Statistical Inference).
If we observe \(n\) sessions, before seeing the results we can represent them by
\[
X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_n.
\]
After those sessions actually happen, we observe concrete values:
\[
x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n.
\]
In practice, these observed values are stored as data — that is, as a dataset (in this case with only one column).

This is an important connection between the language of theory and what we see in practice. In our example, the whole path can be seen at once:
\[
\begin{array}{c}
\boxed{X\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p),\quad p\text{ unknown}} \\
\Downarrow \\
\boxed{X_1,\ldots,X_n\quad \text{(the sample, before observation)}} \\
\Downarrow \\
\boxed{\text{we observe their values}} \\
\Downarrow \\
\boxed{x_1,\ldots,x_n\quad \text{(observed dataset)}} \\
\Downarrow \\
\boxed{\text{we use the data to learn about }p}
\end{array}
\]
That is: what in theory we write as \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) becomes, after observation, the concrete values \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) that we find in a dataset. From there, we use what we observed to learn about what we do not know.
Here Statistical Inference begins:

we start from the observed data to learn about unknown characteristics of the probability model; but we continue to use mathematics and Probability Theory to formalize the idea of inference.







Probability does not disappear



Statistical Inference does not replace Probability.
It depends on it.
We continue using a probabilistic structure to represent the mechanism that could have generated the data. The difference is that now some part of that structure is unknown and must be learned from the observations.

title: The Map of Probability and Inference
text:
But what about Descriptive Statistics?
So far we have talked about Probability and Statistical Inference. But there is a third term that appears all the time in books, courses, and data work: Descriptive Statistics.
The idea is much simpler than the name may suggest.
After we observe the values
\[
x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n,
\]
and have a dataset in hand, we can simply ask:

What do these data that I observed show?

For example:

what was the observed conversion rate?
what was the average spending?
what was the median?
how are the values distributed?
are there values far from the others?
what is the observed correlation between two columns?

This is the role of Descriptive Statistics: to organize, summarize, and visualize the data we actually observed.
\[
\begin{array}{c}
\boxed{\text{observed dataset}} \\
\Downarrow \\
\boxed{\text{summarize and describe what happened in the data}}
\end{array}
\]
Suppose, for example, that we observed 1,000 checkout sessions and in 120 of them there was a purchase.
The observed conversion rate is
\[
\frac{120}{1000}=0.12.
\]
Saying

“12% of the sessions in this dataset ended in purchase”

is a purely descriptive statement. We are simply summarizing what happened in the data we have in hand.
Notice that, in order to make this statement, we still do not need to say that \(0.12\) is the true conversion probability of all users, nor that this number will repeat in another set of sessions.
To try to go beyond the observed dataset, we need something more. That is exactly where the probability model and Statistical Inference come in.
crumbs: 3  The Map of Probability and Inference

title: The Map of Probability and Inference
section: The map we want to keep
text:
The map we want to keep
Everything in this prelude can be summarized in a single map.
The first movement is that of Probability Theory: the real world motivates the construction of a mathematical representation for uncertain phenomena.
\[
\begin{array}{c}
\boxed{\text{uncertain real phenomenon}} \\
\Downarrow \\
\boxed{\text{aggregate regularities}} \\
\Downarrow \\
\boxed{\begin{array}{c}
\text{probability model} \\
\text{(mathematics!)}
\end{array}}
\end{array}
\]
When the model is completely specified, we follow the direction of Probability Theory:
\[
\boxed{\text{specified probability model}}
\;\longrightarrow\;
\boxed{\text{possible data and their probabilities}}
\]
The second movement is that of Statistical Inference. When some characteristic of the model is unknown, we observe a sample:
\[
\begin{array}{c}
\boxed{X_1,\ldots,X_n} \\
\Downarrow \\
\boxed{\text{we observe}} \\
\Downarrow \\
\boxed{x_1,\ldots,x_n} \\
\Downarrow \\
\boxed{\text{observed dataset}}
\end{array}
\]
And, from this dataset, two different questions appear:
\[
\begin{array}{ccc}
& \boxed{\text{observed dataset}} & \\
& \boxed{x_1,\ldots,x_n} & \\
& \swarrow \qquad \searrow & \\
\boxed{\text{DESCRIPTIVE STATISTICS}}
&&
\boxed{\text{STATISTICAL INFERENCE}}
\\[0.15cm]
\Downarrow && \Downarrow
\\[0.15cm]
\boxed{\text{describe what we observed}}
&&
\boxed{\begin{array}{c}
\text{use data + probability model}\\
\text{to learn about unknown}\\
\text{characteristics of the mechanism}
\end{array}}
\end{array}
\]
In one sentence for each part:

Descriptive Statistics: what happened in the data we observed?
Probability Theory: if this is the probabilistic mechanism, what could happen and with what probabilities?
Statistical Inference: what do the observed data, together with a probability model, allow us to learn about the mechanism that could have produced them?

These three ideas do not compete with one another. In practice, a Data Scientist may describe and explore the data, build or evaluate a model, and do inference — often moving back and forth between these steps.
But, conceptually, it is worth keeping the distinction:

describing the data is not the same as inferring beyond them.

With this map in mind, we can return to the beginning and ask the first question of the course:

why do we need a Theory of Probability?

And those are “Scenes from the next chapter…”
crumbs: 3  The Map of Probability and Inference

title: Empirical Modeling: from the Real World to the Statistical Model
text:
The statistical model inside a larger process
In the first prelude, we saw the general map connecting Probability, data, and Statistical Inference.
Now let us move one level up.
Before asking how to construct a probability space, a random variable, or a distribution, it is worth asking:
A useful answer is: to do empirical modeling — that is, to build and use models in order to learn, in a disciplined way, about phenomena observed in the real world from data.
A statistical model is a probabilistic representation of the phenomenon we want to study.
But building a model does not finish the job.
In empirical modeling, the model enters a larger process:
\[
\begin{array}{c}
\boxed{\textbf{REAL WORLD}}\\
\Downarrow\\
\boxed{\text{stochastic phenomenon}}\\
\Downarrow\\
\boxed{
\begin{array}{c}
\textbf{EMPIRICAL MODELING}\\[0.4em]
\text{specify}\\
\Downarrow\\
\text{estimate}\\
\Downarrow\\
\text{confront with the data}\\
\Downarrow\\
\text{revise when necessary}
\end{array}}
\end{array}
\]
crumbs: 4  Empirical Modeling: from the Real World to the Statistical Model

title: Empirical Modeling: from the Real World to the Statistical Model
text:
The four stages
In the organization we will follow, this process can be thought of as four movements.
\[
\boxed{\textbf{1. SPECIFICATION}}
\]
We choose a probabilistic representation for the phenomenon.
This involves questions such as:

what do we want to explain or measure?
which variables enter?
what type of relationship are we assuming?
what probabilistic assumptions are we making?

\[
\Downarrow
\]
\[
\boxed{\textbf{2. ESTIMATION}}
\]
We use the observed data to learn unknown values of the model.
This is where ideas such as parameters, estimators, and fitting procedures appear.
\[
\Downarrow
\]
\[
\boxed{\textbf{3. MISSPECIFICATION CHECKING}}
\]
We ask whether the model we posited is compatible with relevant aspects of the data.
In language closer to day-to-day Data Science, this is where ideas such as these appear:

diagnostics;
residual analysis;
assumption checking;
validation;
model checking.

\[
\Downarrow
\]
\[
\boxed{\textbf{4. RESPECIFICATION}}
\]
If the model does not adequately capture the observed structure, we revise it.
We may change variables, relationships, distributions, assumptions, or even the entire class of model.






We do not need to master any of these stages right now.
The goal is to realize that specifying a model is only the beginning.
Later on, we will need to know how to build, estimate, evaluate, and, when necessary, revise models.
crumbs: 4  Empirical Modeling: from the Real World to the Statistical Model

title: Empirical Modeling: from the Real World to the Statistical Model
text:
A simple example: regression
Imagine that we want to study customer spending using some observed characteristics.
We can begin by specifying something like
\[
Y_i
=
\beta_0
+
\beta_1X_{1i}
+
\beta_2X_{2i}
+
\varepsilon_i
\]
where \(Y_i\) represents spending and the \(X\)’s represent customer characteristics.
Even before calculating anything, we have already made several choices.

1. Specification
At this first stage, we choose:

what the variable of interest is;
which variables to use to represent it;
a functional form;
and a probabilistic structure for the problem.

In other words, before fitting any model, we already need to decide how we will represent the phenomenon.


2. Estimation
Then we use the data to obtain values such as
\[
\hat\beta_0,\hat\beta_1,\hat\beta_2.
\]
This is where the model meets the data: we use the observed sample to learn unknown values of the model.


3. Model checking
But the work is not over yet.
After estimating, we may discover that:

the residuals have structure;
the relationship does not seem linear;
different groups behave in different ways;
or some model assumption seems implausible.

In other words, we need to ask whether the model we chose seems compatible with the observed data.


4. Respecification
If the answer is “not completely,” we may need to:

add an interaction;
transform a variable;
include new predictors;
or even choose another representation for the problem.

That is, the model may need to be revised.






Read this example as a cycle



\[
\boxed{\text{1. Specification}}
\longrightarrow
\boxed{\text{2. Estimation}}
\longrightarrow
\boxed{\text{3. Model\ Checking}}
\longrightarrow
\boxed{\text{4. Respecification}}
\]
Even an apparently simple regression already participates in this cycle.
crumbs: 4  Empirical Modeling: from the Real World to the Statistical Model

title: Empirical Modeling: from the Real World to the Statistical Model
text:
And in Causal Inference?
The same logic appears even more explicitly when we want to answer a causal question.
Imagine that we want to study:

what is the effect of a campaign on customer spending?


1. Specification
Before estimating any effect, we need to specify the problem.
This involves questions such as:

what is the treatment?
what is the outcome?
what is the population?
what effect do we want to estimate?
which assumptions make this comparison causal?

That is, before any calculation, we need to make clear what the causal question is and under what conditions it can be answered.


2. Estimation
Then we use the data to estimate the effect of interest.
Depending on the problem, this may involve regression, matching, weighting, Difference-in-Differences, experiments, or other methods.


3. Model checking
Next, we need to evaluate whether the relevant assumptions seem plausible and whether the procedure is working as expected.
Checks such as the following may appear:

balance;
overlap;
pre-trends;
residual diagnostics;
placebo tests;
sensitivity checks.



4. Respecification
If some assumption or important aspect of the model does not seem adequate, we need to revise the strategy.
This may mean:

changing the specification;
adjusting the set of covariates;
switching methods;
redefining the population;
or reformulating the causal question itself.







The same cycle appears again



\[
\boxed{\text{1. Specification}}
\longrightarrow
\boxed{\text{2. Estimation}}
\longrightarrow
\boxed{\text{3. Model\ Checking}}
\longrightarrow
\boxed{\text{4. Respecification}}
\]
The difference is that, in Causal Inference, the assumptions needed to interpret the result causally take on a central role.


Again, we do not need to learn these tools now.
The point is to realize where the foundations of this course are taking us.
crumbs: 4  Empirical Modeling: from the Real World to the Statistical Model

title: Empirical Modeling: from the Real World to the Statistical Model
text:
And Machine Learning?
There is a clear relationship, but it is not a perfect equivalence.
In a predictive Machine Learning problem, we also choose a representation, fit the model, evaluate its performance, and iterate:
\[
\boxed{\text{choose}}
\longrightarrow
\boxed{\text{train}}
\longrightarrow
\boxed{\text{validate}}
\longrightarrow
\boxed{\text{revise}}
\]
So the general logic remains useful.
But the focus of this course is closer to Statistical Modeling, Econometrics, Experimentation, and Causal Inference, where explicitly understanding the probabilistic structure and the assumptions of the model will be especially important.






Why does this matter for a Data Scientist?



Because knowing how to execute
model.fit(X, y)
is only one part of the problem.
Before fit, someone needed to decide what is being modeled, under what assumptions, and with what structure.
After fit, someone still needs to decide whether what was estimated answers the original question and whether the model is compatible with the data.
crumbs: 4  Empirical Modeling: from the Real World to the Statistical Model

title: Empirical Modeling: from the Real World to the Statistical Model
text:
Where are we going?
We can now put the whole architecture in a single figure:
\[
\begin{array}{c}
\boxed{\textbf{REAL WORLD}}\\
\Downarrow\\
\boxed{\text{stochastic phenomenon}}\\
\Downarrow\\
\boxed{
\begin{array}{c}
\textbf{EMPIRICAL MODELING}\\[0.3em]
\text{specify}\\
\rightarrow
\text{estimate}\\
\rightarrow
\text{check}\\
\rightarrow
\text{revise}
\end{array}}
\\
\Uparrow\\[-0.2em]
\textit{uses}\\
\Uparrow\\
\boxed{\textbf{STATISTICAL MODEL}}\\
\Uparrow\\[-0.2em]
\textit{but how do we build this object?}\\
\Uparrow\\
\boxed{\text{we will begin with the simplest case}}\\
\Uparrow\\
\boxed{\textbf{RANDOM EXPERIMENT}}
\end{array}
\]
That last question will be the theme of the next prelude.
To understand where a statistical model comes from, we will go back to the beginning and build, step by step, the probabilistic structure of the simplest case.






The next step



In the next prelude, we will go one level deeper into this architecture:
\[
\boxed{\text{random experiment}}
\longrightarrow
\boxed{\text{probability theory}}
\longrightarrow
\boxed{\text{statistical space}}
\longrightarrow
\boxed{\text{random variables}}
\longrightarrow
\boxed{\text{statistical model}}
\]
After that, we will begin building each piece for real.
crumbs: 4  Empirical Modeling: from the Real World to the Statistical Model

title: Where We Want to Go: from the Random Experiment to the Statistical Model
text:
From the stochastic phenomenon to the random experiment
In the two previous preludes, we built the broader context of this journey.
First we saw the general map connecting Probability, data, and Statistical Inference.
Then we saw that these objects are part of a larger process of empirical modeling: specifying models, estimating them, confronting them with the data, and revising them when necessary.
Now we will go one level deeper into the architecture:
To answer, we will begin with the simplest mathematical structure we will use to represent a stochastic phenomenon: the random experiment.
This question organizes a large part of the road ahead.
The strategy will be to begin with the simplest possible case, understand its architecture precisely, and only then expand that architecture to more realistic phenomena.
This is important because, in the next chapters, we will start working with symbols such as \(\Omega\), \(\mathcal F\), \(P\), Cartesian products, and sequences of trials. If we look only at each isolated piece, it is easy to lose sight of what we are building and why.
The idea of this prelude is to see the forest first. Later we will enter the trees.
We begin in the real world with a stochastic phenomenon: a phenomenon in which there is uncertainty about individual realizations, but regularities may appear when we observe many occurrences.
This is the combination we already called chance regularity:
\[
\boxed{\text{individual uncertainty}}
\qquad + \qquad
\boxed{\text{aggregate regularity}}
\]
But stochastic phenomena can have very different structures. Therefore, instead of trying to begin with the most general case, we will begin with a particularly simple class.
The idea is to represent a phenomenon that can be thought of as a random experiment.
Here, random experiment does not mean only “something uncertain that happens.” It is a chance mechanism with three specific characteristics:
Simple examples fit this idea well: tossing a coin, measuring the lifetime of a light bulb, or counting how many calls arrive at a call center during a time interval.
The last situation already seems much closer to real data. Even so, if we can imagine the count being observed repeatedly under sufficiently similar conditions, it can initially be treated within this simple structure.
Not every stochastic phenomenon, however, fits this structure.
Think, for example, of a time series of exchange rates. The possible values can be described and the next value is uncertain, but condition [c] is problematic: circumstances change over time and today’s value may be related to yesterday’s. The phenomenon remains stochastic and may exhibit chance regularity, but the simple structure of the random experiment is no longer sufficient to capture it.
That is,
\[
\boxed{\text{stochastic phenomenon}}
\quad \not\Rightarrow \quad
\boxed{\text{simple random experiment}}
\]
This contrast is important for understanding the strategy of the course:
crumbs: 5  Where We Want to Go: from the Random Experiment to the Statistical Model

title: Where We Want to Go: from the Random Experiment to the Statistical Model
text:
[a] The possible outcomes are known a priori.
[b] The result of a particular trial is not known a priori, but there is a regularity of occurrence associated with the outcomes.
[c] The experiment can be repeated under identical conditions.









Why begin with such a simple case?



Because it allows us to build, without unnecessary complications, the fundamental architecture of the theory.
First we mathematize a simple form of stochastic phenomenon. Then we will see which assumptions need to be modified when the real phenomenon is more complex.








we will begin by building the model of the simple case precisely; then we will have a foundation on which to introduce dependence, heterogeneity, and more realistic structures.


The three conditions will be our roadmap
The mathematical formalization will follow directly from the three characteristics of the random experiment:
\[
\begin{array}{rcl}
\textbf{[a]} & \text{which outcomes are possible?} & \longrightarrow \Omega \\\[0.8em]
\textbf{[b]} & \text{how do we represent uncertainty?} & \longrightarrow (\Omega,\mathcal F,P) \\\[0.8em]
\textbf{[c]} & \text{how do we represent its repetitions?} & \longrightarrow \mathcal G_n
\end{array}
\]
This is the common thread of the next chapters.
In other words, we are trying to mathematize the random experiment. The first complete form of that formalization will be a statistical space. Later, with random variables, we will arrive at the numerical form that we will call a statistical model.
crumbs: 5  Where We Want to Go: from the Random Experiment to the Statistical Model

title: Where We Want to Go: from the Random Experiment to the Statistical Model
section: First destination: building the abstract spaces
text:
First destination: building the abstract spaces
The first question will lead us to the set of possible outcomes:
\[
\boxed{\Omega}
\]
Then we will build the events we want to represent and a function capable of assigning probabilities to them:
\[
\boxed{(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)}
\]
This object will be called a probability space.
It represents mathematically the uncertainty associated with the outcome of one complete trial of the experiment we defined.
But our story does not end with one trial.
If we perform the experiment several times,
\[
T_1,T_2,\ldots,T_n,
\]
we will need to represent jointly the possible outcomes of those executions and the probabilistic structure that exists among them.
This will lead us to a joint probability space,
\[
(\Omega^{(n)},\mathcal F^{(n)},P^{(n)}),
\]
and to the sampling space
\[
\mathcal G_n.
\]
Putting these pieces together, we will arrive at our first major destination:
\[
\boxed{
\left[
(\Omega^{(n)},\mathcal F^{(n)},P^{(n)}),
\mathcal G_n
\right]
}
\]
which we will call a statistical space.






What are we building up to this point?



An abstract mathematical structure capable of representing:

the uncertainty of a trial;
several executions of the experiment;
and the probabilistic relationship among those executions.

We are still working with spaces, events, and probability functions — not with the numerical data that will appear later.



And where does IID fit in?
In the simple construction motivating this story, the expression “repeat under identical conditions” will eventually lead to the IID case.
In our course, however, we will make a small pedagogical generalization: first we will build a general sampling space \(\mathcal G_n\) and only later specialize to the case in which the trials are modeled as:

[I] being independent;
[ID] identically distributed, that is, with the same probabilistic structure.

In that case, we will arrive at the simple structure
\[
\boxed{
\left[
(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)^n,
\mathcal G_n^{IID}
\right]
}
\]
which will be called the simple statistical space.
We do not need to understand IID now.
The important thing to keep in mind is only this:

IID does not appear because there are many data points. It is an additional assumption about how we model the relationship among the trials.

Later we will see that formalizing precisely the idea that “knowing what happened in one trial does not change the probabilities of the others” will require a new tool: conditional probability.
Attention: conditional probability is a general concept and does not depend on repeated trials. It appears here in our narrative because it will be a natural tool for defining independence.
crumbs: 5  Where We Want to Go: from the Random Experiment to the Statistical Model

title: Where We Want to Go: from the Random Experiment to the Statistical Model
text:
Spaces now, models later
Here is a distinction that will be fundamental so that we do not mix different stages of the construction:
\[
\boxed{\textbf{SPACE} \neq \textbf{MODEL}}
\]
Up to the end of this first part, we will be building abstract spaces.
Only afterwards will we introduce random variables. They will allow us to take this abstract structure to numerical objects defined on the real line.
We can visualize the transformation like this:
\[
\begin{array}{ccc}
\boxed{
\begin{array}{c}
\textbf{NOW}\\[0.3em]
\text{probability space}\\
(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\\[0.6em]
+\\[0.6em]
\text{sampling space}\\
\mathcal G_n\\[0.6em]
\Downarrow\\
\textbf{statistical space}
\end{array}}
&
\quad \xrightarrow{\quad \text{random variables} \quad} \quad
&
\boxed{
\begin{array}{c}
\textbf{LATER}\\[0.3em]
\text{probability model}\\
\textit{(probability model)}\\[0.6em]
+\\[0.6em]
\text{sampling model}\\
\textit{(sampling model)}\\[0.6em]
\Downarrow\\
\textbf{statistical model}
\end{array}}
\end{array}
\]
The idea is simple:
\[
\boxed{\text{abstract structure}}
\quad\longrightarrow\quad
\boxed{\text{numerical representation}}
\]
The probability space \((\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\) will be carried, through random variables, to a probability model.
In the same way, the structure of the trials will be carried to a sampling model.
The two sides will then form a statistical model.






But we already used the word model in the previous prelude…



Yes — and that was intentional.
First we showed the destination to build a general intuition. Now we will begin to distinguish the stages of the road more precisely.
In the next chapters, \((\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\) will be called a probability space. The probability model, in the more specific sense we will adopt later, will appear only after we introduce random variables and distributions.
crumbs: 5  Where We Want to Go: from the Random Experiment to the Statistical Model

title: Where We Want to Go: from the Random Experiment to the Statistical Model
section: The complete map of the construction
text:
The complete map of the construction
We can now look at the whole story at once:
\[
\begin{array}{c}
\boxed{\text{REAL WORLD}}\\
\Downarrow\\
\boxed{\text{stochastic phenomenon}}\\
\Downarrow\\[-0.2em]
\textit{we begin with the simplest case}\\
\Downarrow\\
\boxed{\text{random experiment: [a], [b], [c]}}\\
\Downarrow\\[-0.2em]
\text{mathematical formalization}\\
\Downarrow\\
\boxed{
\begin{array}{c}
\Omega,\ \mathcal F,\ P,\ \mathcal G_n\\[0.3em]
\textbf{STATISTICAL SPACE}
\end{array}}
\\[1em]
\textit{later}\\[-0.2em]
\Downarrow\\
\boxed{\text{random variables}}\\
\Downarrow\\
\boxed{\textbf{STATISTICAL MODEL}}\\
\Downarrow\\
\boxed{\text{observed data and inference}}
\end{array}
\]
Notice that the random experiment is not a set containing these spaces.
It is the conceptual mechanism we are trying to represent. The spaces appear as part of its mathematical formalization.
crumbs: 5  Where We Want to Go: from the Random Experiment to the Statistical Model

title: Where We Want to Go: from the Random Experiment to the Statistical Model
text:
Where will the data appear?
When we arrive at random variables, the trials
\[
T_1,T_2,\ldots,T_n
\]
can be associated with numerical objects
\[
X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_n.
\]
After the trials actually occur, we will observe concrete values
\[
x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n.
\]
That is when we will begin to recognize what, in the real world, we store as data.
For example, imagine that our interest is to observe the spending of different customers in a purchase. After observing the customers, we might end up with something like this:

In this example,
\[
x_1 = 42.90,\qquad
x_2 = 18.50,\qquad
x_3 = 76.20,\qquad
x_4 = 31.00,\qquad \ldots
\]
Each \(x_i\) is therefore an observed value: what actually appeared after the corresponding trial took place.
It is precisely the collection of these observed values that we begin to recognize, in the day-to-day of Data Science, as a dataset.
So the general idea is:
\[
\boxed{
T_1,\ldots,T_n
\quad\longrightarrow\quad
X_1,\ldots,X_n
\quad\longrightarrow\quad
x_1,\ldots,x_n
\quad\longrightarrow\quad
\text{observed dataset}
}
\]
Later on, we will see carefully how we move from each trial \(T_i\) to a random variable \(X_i\), and from \(X_i\) to the observed value \(x_i\).
But we do not need to formalize that step yet.
For now, it is enough to know where it will appear.






Read this map like this



We begin by mathematizing the simplest form of the stochastic phenomenon: the random experiment.
First we will build its abstract structure. Then we will use random variables to transform it into numerical objects. Only then will we be ready to connect this structure to data — and, later on, to expand the model when the real world requires dependence, heterogeneity, and other forms of complexity.


In the next chapters, we will follow exactly this path — one piece at a time.

title: From Uncertainty to Probability
text:
Deterministic vs. stochastic
In the prelude, we saw the overall map: real-world phenomena produce data, and we use Probability to construct a mathematical representation of the mechanism capable of generating them.
But before calculating probabilities, we need to answer:
The answer begins with the type of phenomenon we want to represent.
Consider \(y=f(x)=2x+1\).
If \(x=3\), then necessarily \(y=7\).
Given \(x\) and the mechanism \(f\), the result is determined.
This is a deterministic phenomenon.
Now think of a user’s checkout session on an e-commerce platform.
We may know the device, country, time, products in the cart, and several other characteristics of the user.
Even so, we do not necessarily know whether the user will make a purchase.
The outcome may be:
\[
\text{purchase}
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
\text{no purchase}.
\]
There is uncertainty about the outcome that will be observed.
This is the type of situation we will call a stochastic phenomenon.
But this does not mean an absence of structure.

title: From Uncertainty to Probability
text: In a stochastic phenomenon, we cannot determine in advance which particular outcome will be observed.

title: From Uncertainty to Probability
text:
Chance and regularity
Spanos1 uses the expression chance regularity to describe a fundamental characteristic of stochastic phenomena:
\[
\underbrace{\text{Chance}}_{\text{individual uncertainty}}
+
\underbrace{\text{Regularity}}_{\text{aggregate structure}}.
\]
In words:

uncertainty in the individual outcome, regularity when we observe many outcomes.

Consider rolling two dice.
On a single roll, the sum can be any value between \(2\) and \(12\), and we do not know in advance which will be observed.

title: From Uncertainty to Probability
text:
Repetition and frequency
Now imagine rolling the two dice many times:
\[
7,\;4,\;10,\;6,\;7,\;9,\;3,\;8,\ldots
\]
Each individual outcome remains uncertain, but we can observe how many times a particular event occurs.
If the sum \(7\) appears \(18\) times in \(100\) rolls, its observed relative frequency will be
\[
\frac{18}{100}=0.18.
\]
If we repeat the process, we may obtain \(0.15\), \(0.19\), \(0.17,\ldots\)
These frequencies vary, but they may exhibit regularity as the number of observations increases.
This is precisely the combination:
\[
\boxed{
\text{individual uncertainty}
+
\text{aggregate regularity}
}
\]






Probability is not relative frequency



Relative frequency is something we observe in the data.
Probability will be part of the mathematical model we construct.
Later, the Law of Large Numbers (LLN) will establish the relationship between these two ideas under certain conditions.

section: From the phenomenon to the data
text:
From the phenomenon to the data
In the real world, we generally do not observe the stochastic mechanism directly; we observe its realizations.
In a checkout session, for example, we may observe:

This forces us to distinguish between two things:

The data are what we observe. The underlying mechanism is what we want to represent mathematically.
Later, we will call this mechanism the Data-Generating Process, or DGP.

title: From Uncertainty to Probability
From Uncertainty to Probability
text:
Before moving on
So far, we have established the motivation: stochastic phenomena combine uncertainty in the individual outcome with some kind of structure or regularity.
The next step is to turn this intuition into mathematics.
In the next chapter, we will begin the formalization: we will see how to define precisely the phenomenon we want to study and how to organize the mathematical objects that will allow us to move from Probability to Statistics.

The question is no longer simply “why Probability?” It becomes: how do we construct a mathematical model to represent this uncertainty?

title: Mathematical Formalization - Statistical Space
Mathematical Formalization - Statistical Space
Mathematical Formalization - Statistical Space
text:
The first part: Probability Space
Conditions [a] and [b] are formalized by the Probability Space.
For a single trial:
\[
(\Omega,\mathcal F,P).
\]
Here:

\(\Omega\) contains the possible outcomes;
\(\mathcal F\) organizes the questions we want to ask about these outcomes;
\(P\) assigns probabilities to these questions.

When we want to represent several trials jointly, we use the corresponding structure
\[
(\Omega^{(n)},\mathcal F^{(n)},P^{(n)}).
\]
The idea is the same. We are now describing the possible outcomes of the \(n\) trials jointly in probabilistic terms.

title: Mathematical Formalization - Statistical Space
text:
The second part: Sampling Space
Condition [c] introduces a second structure.
If we repeat the experiment \(n\) times, we write
\[
\mathcal G_n=\{T_1,T_2,\ldots,T_n\},
\]
where \(T_i\) represents the \(i\)th trial.
We will call \(\mathcal G_n\) the Sampling Space.
At this point, it simply organizes the sequence of trials.
We are not yet assuming that these trials are independent or identically distributed.
Therefore:

\(T_i\) = trial;
\(\omega_i\) = outcome of trial \(T_i\);
\(\Omega\) = sample space;
\(\mathcal G_n\) = sampling space.

These last two objects have similar names, but they represent different things.

title: Mathematical Formalization - Statistical Space
text:
Putting the two parts together
We can now see the complete mathematical representation.


  
    Random Experiment
  

  
    mathematical representation
  

  
    \(\downarrow\)
  

  
    
      Statistical Space
    

    

      
        Probability Space
        formalizes [a] and [b]
        \((\Omega^{(n)},\mathcal F^{(n)},P^{(n)})\)
      

      
        Sampling Space
        formalizes [c]
        \(\mathcal G_n=\{T_1,T_2,\ldots,T_n\}\)
      

    
  

Thus, in the general case:
\[
\boxed{
\left[
(\Omega^{(n)},\mathcal F^{(n)},P^{(n)}),
\quad
\mathcal G_n
\right]
}
\]
is the abstract structure we will use to represent uncertainty and repetition of the experiment jointly.

This is exactly what we are doing now: building the necessary language so that, later on, concepts in Statistics and Causal Inference do not appear as isolated formulas.

title: Part 1 of 2 - Constructing a Probability Space
text:
1. What can happen in a trial of an experiment? (\(\Omega\))
In the previous chapter, we started with a Random Experiment and began constructing its mathematical representation.
The overall architecture is:
\[
\boxed{\text{Random Experiment}}
\longrightarrow
\boxed{\text{mathematical representation}}
\longrightarrow
\boxed{\text{Statistical Space}}
\]
The Statistical Space organizes this formalization into two parts:
In this chapter, we will open only the first box.
We continue formalizing the same Random Experiment, but now we will examine in detail the structure responsible for conditions [a] and [b]:
This structure is the Probability Space:
\[
\boxed{(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)}
\]
We will construct it by answering three questions:
For now, we will remain entirely within this first box. The formalization of repeated trials of the experiment will come in the next step.
We begin by defining the experiment.
An experiment is the procedure whose outcome we want to model.
When we carry out this procedure once, we perform a trial.
At the end of a trial, something has happened.
The complete outcome of that trial, called an elementary outcome, is denoted by \(\omega\), while the set of all possible outcomes is denoted by \(\Omega\).
For example, if the experiment is
one possible elementary outcome is \(\omega=4\).
Thus, the set \(\Omega\) of all possible elementary outcomes is called the sample space:
\[
\boxed{
\Omega=\{\text{all possible elementary outcomes of the experiment}\}
}
\]
Therefore, an element of this set is represented by
\[
\boxed{
\omega\in\Omega
}
\]
In other words:
When rolling a die,
\[
\Omega=\{1,2,3,4,5,6\},
\]
and, after one trial, we might observe, for example,
\[
\omega=4.
\]

title: Part 1 of 2 - Constructing a Probability Space
text:
rolling a die once,








\(\omega\) represents one specific possibility;
\(\Omega\) represents the set of all possibilities.






The form of \(\Omega\) depends on how we define the experiment
The sample space must represent everything we want to observe at the end of a trial.
If the experiment produces only one piece of information, an elementary outcome \(\omega\) may have a single coordinate.
For example:

tossing a coin once.

In this case, \(\Omega=\{H,T\}\) and one possible outcome is \(\omega=H\).
Now suppose the experiment is:

tossing a coin twice and recording the order.

A trial now ends only after both tosses.
Therefore, each elementary outcome must record two pieces of information: \(\Omega=\{(H,H),(H,T),(T,H),(T,T)\}\)
For example, \(\omega=(H,T)\).
This is still a single elementary outcome of a single trial.
The same applies if the experiment is:

rolling two dice and recording the result of each die separately.

If \(\Omega_1=\Omega_2=\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}\), then \(\Omega=\Omega_1\times\Omega_2\).
The Cartesian product simply allows us to construct a space whose outcomes have multiple coordinates.
For example, \(\omega=(2,5)\) means that the first die showed \(2\) and the second showed \(5\). The same principle appears in real-world problems.
Imagine a user reaching the checkout page.
If we only want to record

was a purchase made?

we can use \(\Omega=\{\text{purchase},\text{no purchase}\}\).
But if we also want to record the payment method, the outcome must retain more information.
Suppose, for example, that there are two possible payment methods: card or Pix.
In this case, we could define
\[
\Omega=
\{
(\text{purchase},\text{card}),
(\text{purchase},\text{Pix}),
(\text{no purchase},\text{no payment})
\}.
\]
One possible elementary outcome would be \(\omega=(\text{purchase},\text{card})\).
Now each \(\omega\) preserves two pieces of information about the trial: whether a purchase was made and, if so, which payment method was used.






The central idea



The number of coordinates of \(\omega\) depends on how we define a trial of the experiment and which information we want to preserve in the outcome.
Having multiple coordinates does not, in itself, mean that we are dealing with a statistical sample.
Later, when we repeat an experiment \(n\) times to construct a sample, we will use a similar idea — a product space — but this time each coordinate will represent a different trial.




Two important properties of outcomes
For the elementary outcomes in \(\Omega\) to describe the experiment completely and unambiguously, we want two properties:

collectively exhaustive: in a trial of the experiment, some outcome in \(\Omega\) must occur;
mutually exclusive: if one elementary outcome occurs, no other elementary outcome can occur at the same time.

Together, these two ideas say something quite simple:

at the end of a trial, we must be able to point to exactly one \(\omega\in\Omega\), that is, one possible outcome, and say: “this is what happened.”

Since \(\Omega\) is already defined as the set of all possible outcomes, the idea of exhaustiveness is largely built into the definition itself.
The more interesting point to consider is exclusivity: elementary outcomes must be defined without overlap.
Imagine, for example, that we want to model the behavior of a user in an app.
Starting from scratch, we might write:
\[
\Omega=
\{
\text{engaged user},
\text{purchasing user}
\}.
\]
At first glance, this seems reasonable.
But there is a problem: the same user may have engaged and made a purchase.
In this case, at the end of the trial, we cannot point to a single \(\omega\in\Omega\).
Both outcomes could have occurred at the same time.
Therefore, they do not work well as elementary outcomes.
One way to correct this would be to define non-overlapping possibilities:
\[
\Omega=
\{
\text{did not engage and did not purchase},
\text{engaged and did not purchase},
\text{did not engage and purchased},
\text{engaged and purchased}
\}.
\]
Now, at the end of a trial, exactly one of these outcomes occurs.
For example,
\[
\omega=
\text{engaged and purchased}.
\]
This also sets up an important distinction for the next section.
Statements such as

“the user engaged”;
“the user made a purchase”;

can both be true at the same time.
They are therefore better represented as events, that is, sets of elementary outcomes, rather than as elementary outcomes themselves.
When rolling a die,
\[
\Omega=\{1,2,3,4,5,6\},
\]
both properties arise naturally:

the six outcomes cover all possibilities;
at the end of the trial, exactly one face appears.







First piece complete



So far, we have constructed only:
\[
\boxed{\Omega}
\]
We know what can happen.
We have not yet assigned probabilities to anything.

title: Part 1 of 2 - Constructing a Probability Space
section: 2. Which events do we want to ask questions about? (\(\mathcal F\))
text:
2. Which events do we want to ask questions about? (\(\mathcal F\))
An elementary outcome \(\omega\) answers:

what happened?

But our questions usually do not refer to just one outcome.
Consider again
\[
\Omega
=
\{(H,H),(H,T),(T,H),(T,T)\}.
\]
Ask:

did we get exactly one head?

This happens if the outcome is \((H,T)\) or \((T,H)\).
Therefore, we define
\[
A=\{(H,T),(T,H)\}.
\]
This set \(A\) is an event.
In general,
\[
\boxed{
A\subseteq\Omega
}
\]
is an event when it represents a statement that we can answer with yes or no after observing the outcome of the experiment.1
If the observed outcome was
\[
\omega=(H,T),
\]
then
\[
\omega\in A,
\]
and we say that event \(A\) occurred.

Outcomes and events are different objects
It is worth making this distinction visual:



Object
Meaning
Example




\(\omega\)
an elementary outcome
\((H,T)\)


\(\Omega\)
all possible outcomes
\(\{(H,H),(H,T),(T,H),(T,T)\}\)


\(A\)
an event
\(\{(H,T),(T,H)\}\)



Therefore,
\[
\omega\in\Omega
\]
and
\[
A\subseteq\Omega.
\]
We will not confuse a point in the space with a set of points.


Partitions
Before continuing, it is worth introducing a simple idea from Set Theory.
Consider a set \(S\) and several subsets \(A_i\subseteq S\). We say that they form a partition of \(S\) when:

none of them is empty: \(A_i\neq\varnothing\);
they do not overlap: \(A_i\cap A_j=\varnothing\) for \(i\neq j\);
together they cover the entire set: \(\displaystyle\bigcup_i A_i=S\).

Equivalently:

each element of \(S\) belongs to exactly one of the parts.

This is the usual definition of a partition: dividing a set into subsets that do not overlap and leave no element out.2
The figure below helps visualize this idea: the set \(S\) appears as a whole, while each region \(A_i\) represents one part of the partition.


Singleton: a set with a single element
A singleton is simply a set containing exactly one element.
If \(\omega\in\Omega\), then \(\{\omega\}\) is the singleton associated with that elementary outcome. Since \(\{\omega\}\subseteq\Omega\), it is also an event.
A useful connection now emerges: the collection of all singletons
\[
\big\{\{\omega\}:\omega\in\Omega\big\}
\]
forms a partition of \(\Omega\).
When rolling a die, for example,
\[
\Omega=\{1,2,3,4,5,6\},
\]
and the partition into singletons is
\[
\big\{\{1\},\{2\},\{3\},\{4\},\{5\},\{6\}\big\}.
\]
Each outcome belongs to exactly one of these sets.






An important clarification



When we informally say that elementary outcomes partition the sample space, the mathematically precise statement is:

the singleton events associated with the elementary outcomes form a partition of \(\Omega\).






We can combine events
Since events are sets, set operations allow us to combine questions about the same trial.
Consider again
\[
\Omega=\{(H,H),(H,T),(T,H),(T,T)\}.
\]
Define:
\[
A=\{\text{first toss is }H\}
=
\{(H,H),(H,T)\},
\]
and
\[
B=\{\text{second toss is }H\}
=
\{(H,H),(T,H)\}.
\]
Now we can formulate more complex questions.

\(A\cap B\): A and B
Question:

did both the first and second tosses come up heads?

The only outcome satisfying both conditions is
\[
A\cap B=\{(H,H)\}.
\]


\(A\cup B\): A or B
Question:

did at least one of the two tosses come up heads?

This happens in
\[
A\cup B
=
\{(H,H),(H,T),(T,H)\}.
\]


\(A^c\): not A
Question:

did the first toss not come up heads?

Therefore,
\[
A^c
=
\{(T,H),(T,T)\}.
\]
The logic is always the same:

a question about the experiment is represented by the set of all elementary outcomes that would make the answer “yes.”

A single outcome can, naturally, cause several events to occur.
If we observe \(\omega=(H,H)\), then \(\omega\in A\) and \(\omega\in B\). This does not contradict the exclusivity of elementary outcomes: only one outcome occurred, \((H,H)\), but that outcome belongs to several sets representing events.



Why do we need a family of events?
So far, we have transformed different questions into subsets of \(\Omega\).
For example:

“did we get exactly one head?” \(\rightarrow \{(H,T),(T,H)\}\);
“did the first toss come up heads?” \(\rightarrow \{(H,H),(H,T)\}\);
“did at least one toss come up heads?” \(\rightarrow \{(H,H),(H,T),(T,H)\}\).

If we want to assign probabilities to these questions, we need to organize the sets we will accept as events into a single collection.
In mathematics, a collection of sets is often called a family of sets.
We will denote our family of events by
\[
\boxed{\mathcal F}.
\]
Thus, \(\mathcal F\) brings together the events on which our probability function can operate.
There is also a deeper interpretation of this collection.






\(\mathcal F\) can also be interpreted as information



Think again of events as questions with yes-or-no answers.
Then \(\mathcal F\) represents the questions that our space can distinguish and to which we choose to assign probabilistic meaning.
Imagine, for example, an experiment involving five coin tosses, but suppose our system records only the first three. Two outcomes that agree on the first three tosses but differ on the last two will be indistinguishable from the information recorded.
In this case, a question such as

“did at least four heads occur in the five tosses?”

cannot be answered using only the information we decided to observe.
This interpretation helps us see \(\mathcal F\) not as a technical collection invented for convenience, but as a mathematical way of representing which distinctions about the experiment are part of our space.
Later, when we study random variables and conditional probability, this relationship between \(\sigma\)-algebras and information will become even more important.3


But there is a natural requirement: if we can ask certain questions, we also want to combine them without leaving the collection of events.
If \(A\in\mathcal F\), we also want to be able to ask:

“did A not occur?”

Therefore, we need
\[
A^c\in\mathcal F.
\]
If \(A,B\in\mathcal F\), we also want to ask:

“did A or B occur?”

and, therefore,
\[
A\cup B\in\mathcal F.
\]
The same logic applies to intersections, such as “did both A and B occur?”.
We say that the family is closed under these operations — taking the complement of an event, forming unions of events, and intersecting them — because when we combine events that already belong to \(\mathcal F\), the resulting set still belongs to \(\mathcal F\) itself.
A family with the structure required for Probability Theory is called a \(\sigma\)-algebra.






Why the name algebra?



The idea of an algebra here is that we have a collection of sets that remains closed when we apply certain operations to its elements.
It is the same idea as saying, for example, that the integers are closed under addition:
\[
2+3=5,
\]
and the result is still an integer.
But they are not closed under division, because
\[
1/2
\]
is no longer an integer.
In our case, the elements of \(\mathcal F\) are events, that is, sets. We want operations such as complement and union, when applied to events that already belong to \(\mathcal F\), to produce sets that also belong to \(\mathcal F\).
For example:

if \(A\in\mathcal F\), then \(A^c\in\mathcal F\);
if \(A,B\in\mathcal F\), then \(A\cup B\in\mathcal F\).

The intersection also remains in \(\mathcal F\), since it can be constructed from these operations.
The prefix \(\sigma\) adds an important requirement: this closure also applies to countable unions of events, which is relevant when we discuss infinite sample spaces (we will see this later).
For now, the main idea is:

a \(\sigma\)-algebra is a collection of events that remains closed when we apply the set operations needed to formulate new probabilistic questions. Thus, after choosing which basic distinctions are part of the space, we can also consistently represent the questions obtained by combining them.




In the finite case: the power set
In small finite spaces, we can usually simply consider all subsets of \(\Omega\).
For example, if
\[
\Omega=\{H,T\},
\]
we have
\[
2^\Omega
=
\{\varnothing,\{H\},\{T\},\Omega\}.
\]
The object \(2^\Omega\) is called the power set: the collection of all subsets of \(\Omega\).
In this case, we can take
\[
\mathcal F=2^\Omega.
\]
Each element of \(\mathcal F\) corresponds to a possible question:

\(\{H\}\): “did we get heads?”;
\(\{T\}\): “did we get tails?”;
\(\Omega\): “did one of the possible outcomes occur?”;
\(\varnothing\): “did an outcome outside \(\Omega\) occur?”.

This last interpretation leads us to two special events.


Sure event: \(\Omega\)
Consider an ordinary die:
\[
\Omega=\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}.
\]
Ask:

was the outcome a number between 1 and 6?

All possible outcomes make this statement true.
The corresponding event is the sample space itself,
\[
\Omega.
\]
This is why \(\Omega\) is called the sure event. Later we will see that
\[
P(\Omega)=1.
\]


Impossible event: \(\varnothing\)
Now ask:

did the die show 7?

No outcome belonging to \(\Omega\) makes this statement true.
The set of outcomes satisfying the question contains no elements:
\[
\varnothing.
\]
This is why \(\varnothing\) is called the impossible event. Later we will see that
\[
P(\varnothing)=0.
\]
These two cases reinforce the same idea we have been using from the beginning:

an event is the set of all elementary outcomes for which a given question about the experiment is answered “yes.”







For now, just remember the idea



\(\mathcal F\) is the collection of sets to which we will allow probabilities to be assigned.
In the finite case, we can usually work with
\[
\mathcal F=2^\Omega.
\]
In infinite spaces, it will not always be convenient or possible to work with all subsets. This is why the definition in terms of a \(\sigma\)-algebra will become important later.





An important distinction in notation
We now have three different relationships:
\[
\boxed{\omega\in\Omega}
\]
an outcome belongs to the sample space;
\[
\boxed{A\subseteq\Omega}
\]
an event is a subset of the sample space;
\[
\boxed{A\in\mathcal F}
\]
this event belongs to the collection of events to which we can assign probability.






Second piece complete



We now have
\[
\boxed{(\Omega,\mathcal F)}
\]
We know what can happen and which events we can ask probabilistic questions about.
We still need to specify the probability of each event.

title: Part 1 of 2 - Constructing a Probability Space
section: 3. How do we specify and assign probabilities? (\(P\))
text:
3. How do we specify and assign probabilities? (\(P\))
We have finally reached the third piece.
So far, we have constructed:

\(\Omega\): the set of possible elementary outcomes;
\(\mathcal F\): the family of events we want to ask questions about.

Now we need a rule that associates each event with a number between \(0\) and \(1\).
Before discussing Probability, recall the simpler idea of a function.
Suppose we have a discrete domain
\[
D=\{a,b,c\}
\]
and a function
\[
f:D\to\mathbb R.
\]
We can define the rule by saying, for example,
\[
f(a)=2,\qquad f(b)=5,\qquad f(c)=7.
\]
Or visualize it:
\[
\begin{array}{ccc}
a & b & c\\
\downarrow & \downarrow & \downarrow\\
2 & 5 & 7
\end{array}
\]
The function simply determines which output corresponds to each input.
In this example, the domain is \(D\) and the image actually produced by the function is
\[
\operatorname{Im}(f)=\{2,5,7\}.
\]
Now we do exactly the same thing in Probability.
\[
\boxed{
P:\mathcal F\longrightarrow[0,1]
}
\]
The input is now an event \(A\in\mathcal F\), and the function \(P\) determines which number in \([0,1]\) corresponds to that event:
\[
\underbrace{A}_{\text{event}}
\quad\xmapsto{\;P\;}\quad
\underbrace{P(A)}_{\text{probability}}.
\]
An important terminological distinction is worth making here:

\([0,1]\) is the codomain of \(P\);
the image of \(P\) is the set of values it actually takes:

\[
\operatorname{Im}(P)
=
\{P(A):A\in\mathcal F\}
\subseteq[0,1].
\]
In other words, specifying \(P\) means specifying the rule that determines where each event in \(\mathcal F\) is mapped within \([0,1]\).
This function is called a probability law, or, in the language of Measure Theory, a probability measure.

Probability as a measure of sets
Now that \(P\) has appeared, we can answer a question we left open:

why is Probability constructed by assigning numbers to events rather than directly to elementary outcomes?

The first answer is conceptual.
An elementary outcome \(\omega\) describes what happened. An event \(A\subseteq\Omega\) represents a question about what happened.
In the experiment of tossing a coin twice, for example,
\[
\omega=(H,T)
\]
describes a specific outcome, while
\[
A=\{(H,T),(T,H)\}
\]
represents the question:

did we get exactly one head?







Aha moment




the elementary outcome describes what happened; the event represents a question we ask about what happened.

And Probability allows us to quantify the uncertainty associated with precisely these questions:
\[
P(A).
\]


This already makes events useful even before we encounter any difficulties with continuous spaces.

But couldn’t we just work with the points?
In the finite case, we can summarize a probability law by looking at the simplest possible events, the singletons
\[
\{\omega_1\},\{\omega_2\},\ldots,\{\omega_n\}.
\]
After introducing the rules that \(P\) must obey, we will see that the probabilities of these singletons are sufficient to reconstruct the probability of any event in the finite discrete case.
But this is a special case, not a sufficiently general foundation for the entire theory.
In many continuous models,
\[
P(\{\omega\})=0
\]
for every individual outcome \(\omega\), while entire sets of outcomes have positive probability.
More importantly, two different continuous probability laws may assign zero probability to every individual point and still assign different probabilities to the same intervals.
Therefore,

the probabilities of individual points do not, in general, characterize the probability law.

This is where the more general idea emerges:
\[
\boxed{
P:\mathcal F\longrightarrow[0,1]
}
\]
\(P\) is a set function: it measures events.
We do not need to resolve the continuous case now. For now, just remember the architecture:
\[
\begin{array}{c}
\boxed{
\begin{array}{c}
\omega\\
\text{elementary outcome: what happened}
\end{array}
}
\\[8pt]
\Downarrow
\\[8pt]
\boxed{
\begin{array}{c}
A\subseteq\Omega\\
\text{event: a question about what happened}
\end{array}
}
\\[8pt]
\Downarrow
\\[8pt]
\boxed{
\begin{array}{c}
P(A)\\
\text{uncertainty assigned to that question}
\end{array}
}
\end{array}
\]


The connection with Measure Theory
This formulation did not arise by chance.
In the early twentieth century, a powerful analogy became clear: just as we can assign length, area, or volume to sets, we could think of the probability of an event as a kind of measure of its probabilistic size.
Kolmogorov placed this idea at the center of the modern formulation of Probability.4
Bertsekas and Tsitsiklis5 suggest a simple mental image: imagine a total mass of \(1\) distributed over \(\Omega\).
Then \(P(A)\) represents how much of that mass belongs to event \(A\).
But one fundamental question remains:

which rules must a function \(P\) obey to truly be a probability measure?

This is what we formalize now.
