How do we interpret a cell?
Consider
\[
P^{(2)}(H,T)=0.
\]
This means:

under this DGP, the probability that the complete experiment produces the sequence “\(H\) on the first trial and \(T\) on the second trial” is zero.

Now notice something important.
If we look at each trial in isolation, we still have
\[
P_1(H)=P_1(T)=\frac12,
\qquad
P_2(H)=P_2(T)=\frac12.
\]
That is, each trial still looks like a fair coin when observed separately.
But when we look at both jointly, we see information that these individual probabilities do not reveal:

if we know that \(T_1\) resulted in \(H\), we also know that \(T_2\) resulted in \(H\).

Therefore, what changed was the way the two outcomes occur jointly.






We are not yet talking about two random variables



These tables resemble a joint distribution of two random variables, but we are still one step before that.
Here they represent the joint law \(P^{(2)}\) over the possible outcomes of the two trials:
\[
\Omega^{(2)}
=
\{(H,H),(H,T),(T,H),(T,T)\}.
\]
Later, after introducing random variables \(X_1\) and \(X_2\), this same idea will reappear as a joint distribution of random variables.








This can also occur in real-world phenomena



Imagine two parts produced in sequence by the same machine.
If the machine is temporarily out of adjustment, observing a defect in the first part may provide information about the chance that the second part is also defective.
This does not necessarily mean that the defect in the first part causes the defect in the second. The two outcomes may be related because they share part of the same generating mechanism.


Therefore,
\[
\boxed{
\text{probabilities of each trial in isolation}
\;\not\Rightarrow\;
\text{joint law of the sequence}
}
\]
It is precisely the joint law \(P^{(n)}\) that contains information about how the outcomes of different trials occur together.

title: Part 2 of 2 - Sampling Space
text:
The second ingredient: sampling space
Now we give a name to the sequence of trials:
\[
\boxed{
\mathcal G_n=\{T_1,T_2,\ldots,T_n\}.
}
\]
We will call \(\mathcal G_n\) the sampling space.
It identifies the trials we are representing jointly.
Combining
\[
(\Omega^{(n)},\mathcal F^{(n)},P^{(n)})
\]
and
\[
\mathcal G_n,
\]
we obtain the general statistical space:
\[
\boxed{
\left[
(\Omega^{(n)},\mathcal F^{(n)},P^{(n)}),
\mathcal G_n
\right].
}
\]






The sample space is not the sampling space



The sample space \(\Omega\) contains possible outcomes.
The sampling space \(\mathcal G_n\) identifies the sequence of trials under consideration.
And we are not yet talking about a random sample.
That will come later, when we introduce random variables.








What if \(\Omega\) is continuous?



Nothing changes conceptually.
If \(\Omega=\mathbb R\), then \(n\) trials produce elements of
\[
\mathbb R^n.
\]
The rigorous construction of the joint event space uses the product \(\sigma\)-algebra
\[
\mathcal F_1\otimes\cdots\otimes\mathcal F_n,
\]
but we will not develop this technical part here.
The idea remains the same: several trials must live within a joint probabilistic structure.

title: Part 2 of 2 - Sampling Space
text:
What is still missing?
So far, we have not assumed that the trials are independent.
Nor have we assumed that they all have the same distribution.
We have only constructed the structure needed to say:
\[
\boxed{
\text{these trials will be represented jointly}
}
\]
and allow \(P^{(n)}\) to describe how they are related.
In the next chapter, we will ask an additional question:

what do we mean when we say that the same mechanism is repeated “under the same conditions”?

This statement will lead us to two different ideas:

the same probabilistic structure across trials;
the absence of probabilistic influence between them.

To formalize the second, we must first understand an even more basic question:

how does new information change a probability?

This is where conditional probability comes in.

title: Part 2 of 2 - Sampling Space
text:
Before continuing

Why can \((H,T)\) represent either two coordinates of a single trial or outcomes of two different trials?
Why does \(P:\mathcal F\to[0,1]\) not directly answer the question “three heads in five trials”?
What does an element \((\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_n)\in\Omega^{(n)}\) represent in this chapter?
Why does knowing the probabilities of each trial in isolation not determine \(P^{(n)}\)?
What is the difference between the sample space \(\Omega\) and the sampling space \(\mathcal G_n\)?

title: The IID Case
text:
Revisiting the Random Experiment
In the chapter on formalization, we introduced the abstract architecture we are building:
In the previous chapter, we arrived at the general form:
\[
\boxed{
\left[
(\Omega^{(n)},\mathcal F^{(n)},P^{(n)}),
\mathcal G_n
\right].
}
\]
It allows us to represent several trials jointly, but does not yet impose any restrictions on how these trials relate to one another.
At the beginning of the module, we introduced a Random Experiment as a mechanism satisfying three conditions:
The first two ideas are formalized by the Probability Space.
The third is precisely the issue we still need to resolve:
This is where we need to return to the Sampling Space box.

title: The IID Case
text:
we know the possible outcomes;
we do not know in advance which outcome will occur in a trial, but there is probabilistic regularity;
the experiment can be repeated under the same conditions.




what does it mean, mathematically, to repeat the experiment “under the same conditions”?



Reopening the Sampling Space box
So far, we have only a general sequence of trials:
\[
\mathcal G_n=\{T_1,T_2,\ldots,T_n\}.
\]
To represent repetition “under the same conditions”, we will impose two properties:
\[
\boxed{
\begin{array}{c}
\text{same probabilistic structure in each trial}\\
\downarrow\\
\text{Identical Distribution (ID)}
\end{array}
}
\qquad
\boxed{
\begin{array}{c}
\text{one trial provides no information about the others}\\
\downarrow\\
\text{Independence (I)}
\end{array}
}
\]
When both are satisfied,
\[
\boxed{
\mathcal G_n
\quad\xrightarrow{\;\mathrm{ID+I}\;}\quad
\mathcal G_n^{IID}
=
\{T_1,T_2,\ldots,T_n\}.
}
\]
The sequence is then referred to as a sequence of random trials.
Visually, this is the box we are specializing:

  
    
      Sampling Space
    

    
      General case
      \(\mathcal G_n=\{T_1,\ldots,T_n\}\)
    

    
      \(\downarrow\) impose ID + Independence
    

    
      Simple case: Random Trials
      \(\mathcal G_n^{IID}=\{T_1,\ldots,T_n\}\)
    
  

When we combine this box with the probabilistic structure of the outcomes, we obtain the complete abstract formalization of the Random Experiment:

  
    Random Experiment
  
  
    mathematical representation
  
  
    \(\downarrow\)
  

  
    
      Simple Statistical Space
    

    
      
        Probability Space
        outcomes + probabilistic regularity
        \((\Omega,\mathcal F,P)^n\)
      

      
        Simple Sampling Space
        repetition under the same conditions
        \(\mathcal G_n^{IID}=\{T_1,\ldots,T_n\}\)
        Random Trials
      
    
  

Therefore,
\[
\boxed{
\left[
(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)^n,
\quad
\mathcal G_n^{IID}
\right]
}
\]
is the Simple Statistical Space: the abstract formalization of the simplest case of a Random Experiment.
The aim of this chapter is precisely to understand why ID and Independence appear in this second box and what each of these assumptions tells us about the DGP.

title: The IID Case
section: Three dimensions of a probabilistic description of the DGP
text:
Three dimensions of a probabilistic description of the DGP
Before defining ID and Independence, it is worth looking at the broader problem: what do we need to know to describe a stochastic phenomenon probabilistically?
Think about data generated across different trials: customer purchases, sensor measurements, or outcomes observed over time. It is not enough to ask which outcomes are more probable. We also need to ask whether one outcome tells us something about the others and whether the probabilistic behavior remains the same across trials.
This is the central idea behind the framework proposed by Spanos. The patterns of regularity found in stochastic phenomena can be described, in probabilistic terms, by assumptions grouped into three dimensions:









Dimension
Question we ask about the DGP
Intuition: what do we want to find out?




(D) Distribution
How are probabilities distributed among the possible outcomes?
Are some outcomes more probable than others?


(M) Dependence (“Memory”)
Does knowing what happened in one trial change the probabilities of the others?
Does knowing the previous outcome change our probabilities for the next one?


(H) Heterogeneity
Does the probability distribution change from one trial to another?
Do the probabilities remain the same in each trial, or do they change over time?




These three dimensions represent different types of probabilistic information we can use to describe a DGP.
By imposing or relaxing assumptions along these dimensions, we construct more restrictive or more general statistical models, capable of representing different stochastic phenomena.
In this chapter, we will start with a particularly simple case: we will assume Independence (M) and Identical Distribution (H). Together, these two assumptions characterize the IID case.
Later, we will see that not all phenomena satisfy these conditions — and that recognizing dependence and heterogeneity is essential to building models that adequately describe the data.

Why does this distinction matter in practice?
In reality, data do not always behave like a sequence of ordinary coin tosses. Today’s purchases may be related to yesterday’s (dependence); customer profiles may change over the months (heterogeneity); and a heavy-tailed distribution may make a model that assumes a different distributional shape inadequate (distribution).
This is an important source of modeling errors: assuming a simple probabilistic structure without considering whether it represents the phenomenon that generated the data.
For example, when ignored, changes in distribution (data drift) and temporal dependence can undermine the validity of analyses and predictive evaluations.


Where do ID and Independence fit in?
In this chapter, we will study a particularly simple case within this architecture. We leave dimension D arbitrary and impose strong restrictions on the other two:








Dimension
Choice in the simple case (IID)




(D) Distribution
The distribution remains arbitrary: IID does not require a Normal, Bernoulli, or any other specific family.


(M) Dependence
Independence (I): knowing the outcome of one trial does not change our probabilities concerning the others.


(H) Heterogeneity
Identical Distribution (ID): the same probability law describes all trials, that is, complete homogeneity.




Therefore, I and ID are two distinct assumptions, each restricting one dimension of the DGP. By relaxing them, we make room for models that represent dependence and/or heterogeneity, without abandoning probabilistic rigor.
We will start with ID, then develop the intuition behind Independence. Only then will we combine the two conditions to arrive at the IID case.

title: The IID Case
section: 1. (ID) Identical Distribution: the DGP does not change from one trial to another
text:
1. (ID) Identical Distribution: the DGP does not change from one trial to another
Since we are now looking at the trials jointly, we have a joint law \(P^{(n)}\) for the entire sequence.
But we can also look at each position separately. The probability law corresponding to trial \(T_i\) will be denoted by \(P_i\).
This law answers questions about trial \(i\) alone, without having to specify what happened in the other trials.
For example:

what is the probability of obtaining \(H\) on the second toss, regardless of the outcome of the first?

Later, we will refer to this law as the marginal law.

A concrete way to think about this
Suppose that
\[
\Omega=\{H,T\}.
\]
For each trial, we can summarize its probability law using the vector
\[
\mathbf p_i
=
\left[
P_i(\{H\}),
P_i(\{T\})
\right].
\]
If the first trial involves a fair coin,
\[
\mathbf p_1
=
\left[
\tfrac12,\tfrac12
\right].
\]
If we are saying that the same probabilistic mechanism remains in place from one trial to another, then
\[
\boxed{
\mathbf p_1
=
\mathbf p_2
=
\cdots
=
\mathbf p_n
=
\mathbf p.
}
\]
For the fair coin, across all its trials:
\[
\mathbf p_1
=
\mathbf p_2
=
\cdots
=
\mathbf p_n
=
\left[
\tfrac12,\tfrac12
\right].
\]
Here, \(P_i\) is not a number, but a function: the probability law of trial \(i\). As we saw when formalizing the probability space, it takes an event as input and returns its probability:
\[
P_i:\mathcal F_i\longrightarrow[0,1],\qquad A\longmapsto P_i(A).
\]
Therefore, saying that two laws are equal means that these functions assign the same probability to each corresponding event. This is what we mean, at this level, by Identical Distribution (ID):
\[
\boxed{
P_1=P_2=\cdots=P_n=P.
}
\]
Or, writing out the complete structure of each trial,
\[
(\Omega_i,\mathcal F_i,P_i)
=
(\Omega,\mathcal F,P),
\qquad i=1,\ldots,n.
\]
ID does not mean that the observed outcomes are identical. It means that the same probability function describes each trial when considered separately from the others. This equality, by itself, tells us nothing about how the outcomes of different trials relate to one another.
This is the most restrictive form of homogeneity: complete homogeneity.
If, for example,
\[
\mathbf p_1=[0.5,0.5],
\qquad
\mathbf p_2=[0.8,0.2],
\]
the probabilistic mechanism has changed across positions. We have heterogeneity, not ID.
But even knowing that all the marginal laws are equal, one question remains:

how do the outcomes of different trials relate to one another?

title: The IID Case
section: 2. Dependence: does information about one trial change what we know about another?
text:
2. Dependence: does information about one trial change what we know about another?
This brings us to one of the most important ideas in Probability Theory: conditioning.
The intuition is simple:

we have a probabilistic model; we receive new information; should we revise the probabilities we assign to events?

We will use the notation
\[
P(B\mid A)
\]
to represent the probability we assign to \(B\) after learning that \(A\) has occurred.
For now, we do not need the formula for conditional probability. What matters is understanding its purpose: revising probabilities in light of new information.

An example involving a single trial
Consider a fair die.
Before receiving any information,
\[
P(\text{even})=\frac12.
\]
Now someone tells us that the outcome was greater than \(3\).
The only outcomes that are still possible are
\[
\{4,5,6\}.
\]
Two of them are even. Therefore,
\[
P(\text{even}\mid \text{outcome}>3)=\frac23.
\]
The new information has changed our probabilistic assessment.
Conditioning does not require repeated trials. We are simply updating the probabilistic model in light of additional information.


Now return to our trials
Define:

\(A\): “the first trial resulted in \(H\)”;
\(B\): “the second trial resulted in \(H\)”.

The question is:

does knowing that \(A\) occurred change the probability we assign to \(B\)?

This question naturally distinguishes two types of DGP.
In the DGP involving two ordinary tosses of a fair coin,
\[
P^{(2)}(B)=\frac12,
\qquad
P^{(2)}(B\mid A)=\frac12.
\]
Knowing the outcome of the first trial does not change what we expect from the second.
In the DGP constructed in the previous chapter, where the second outcome copies the first,
\[
P^{(2)}(B)=\frac12,
\qquad
P^{(2)}(B\mid A)=1.
\]
Now, information about the first trial completely changes our assessment of the second.
This is the difference we want to capture with the idea of dependence.

title: The IID Case
text:
3. Independence: no revision is necessary
In the simplest case, we want information about one trial to be irrelevant to the others.
Intuitively,
\[
\boxed{
P^{(2)}(B\mid A)=P^{(2)}(B).
}
\]
If knowing that \(A\) occurred does not change the probability we assign to \(B\), we say that the events are independent.

How can we express this idea without using conditioning?
We can think of many repetitions of the mechanism.
Event \(A\) occurs in approximately a proportion \(P(A)\) of the cases.
Now look only at those situations in which \(A\) occurred.
If \(A\) truly provides no information about \(B\), then \(B\) should continue to occur within this subset of cases in the same proportion \(P(B)\) as before.
Therefore, the proportion of situations in which \(A\) and \(B\) occur together should be
\[
P(A)\times P(B).
\]


Visualizing the multiplication rule
A tree helps us see where this product comes from.
In general, to follow the path along which \(A\) occurs and then \(B\) also occurs, we multiply the probabilities along the path:

start
├── A                              P(A)
│   ├── B                          P(B|A)
│   │   └── A and B                P(A) × P(B|A)
│   └── Bᶜ
└── Aᶜ


The general rule is therefore
\[
P(A\cap B)=P(A)\,P(B\mid A).
\]
Now the assumption of independence comes into play.
If knowing that \(A\) occurred does not change our probability for \(B\), then
\[
P(B\mid A)=P(B).
\]
Hence, the second branch of the tree retains exactly the same probability that \(B\) had before we knew anything about \(A\):
\[
P(A\cap B)
=
P(A)\,P(B).
\]
This motivates the mathematical form of independence:
\[
\boxed{
P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B).
}
\]
The equality conveys a very intuitive idea:

to determine the probability that \(A\) and \(B\) occur together, we do not need any additional information about the relationship between them: the individual probabilities are sufficient.

If there is some probabilistic relationship between the events, the second branch will, in general, be \(P(B\mid A)\) rather than simply \(P(B)\). In that case, knowing only \(P(A)\) and \(P(B)\) is not sufficient to determine \(P(A\cap B)\).


Why do we prefer this form as the definition?
The expression
\[
P(B\mid A)=P(B)
\]
is excellent for understanding the idea of independence: knowing \(A\) does not change our probabilities concerning \(B\).
But it requires the conditional probability to be defined.
By contrast,
\[
P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)
\]
is symmetric in \(A\) and \(B\) and remains meaningful even when one of the events has probability zero.
For this reason, we use the product form as the mathematical definition of independence and the conditional form as its intuitive interpretation:
\[
\boxed{
\begin{array}{c}
\text{information about }A\text{ does not change }B\\[4pt]
\Updownarrow\\[4pt]
P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)
\end{array}
}
\]
when the conditional probability involved is well defined.
When we talk about several trials, we want to extend exactly the same idea: knowing the outcomes of some trials should provide no probabilistic information about the others.
In compact form, for events \(E_i\in\mathcal F_i\),
\[
\boxed{
P^{(n)}(E_1\times\cdots\times E_n)
=
P_1(E_1)\cdots P_n(E_n).
}
\]
Independence is therefore an assumption about the joint structure of the DGP.
It does not follow from each trial being fair, nor from the trials having identical distributions.

title: The IID Case
text:
4. ID is not independence
The two assumptions answer different questions:








Assumption
Question




Identical Distribution (ID)
Does the marginal law remain the same from one position to another?


Independence (I)
Does information about one position change the probabilities of the others?




We can have ID with dependence: in the DGP where the second trial copies the first,
\[
P_1(H)=P_2(H)=\frac12,
\]
but knowing the first outcome determines the second.
We can also have independence without ID: for example,
\[
P_1(H)=0.5,
\qquad
P_2(H)=0.8,
\]
even if the mechanism creates no probabilistic relationship between the two outcomes.
Therefore,
\[
\boxed{\mathrm{I}\neq\mathrm{ID}.}
\]

title: The IID Case
text:
5. Combining the two restrictions: IID
We can now formalize the idea of repeating the same experiment under the simplest conditions:

the marginal law does not change across trials — ID;
one trial provides no probabilistic information about the others — I.

Hence,
\[
\boxed{
\underbrace{\text{Independence}}_{\mathrm I}
+
\underbrace{\text{Identical Distribution}}_{\mathrm{ID}}
=
\mathrm{IID}.
}
\]
A sequence
\[
\boxed{
\mathcal G_n^{IID}
=
\{T_1,T_2,\ldots,T_n\}
}
\]
that satisfies these two properties will be called a sequence of random trials.
Since all the marginal laws are equal,
\[
P_1=P_2=\cdots=P_n=P,
\]
and, by independence, the joint law factorizes into these marginal laws.
Thus, the joint structure takes the product form
\[
(\Omega^n,\mathcal F^{\otimes n},P^{\otimes n}),
\]
which we will abbreviate as
\[
(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)^n.
\]
We thus arrive at the simple statistical space:
\[
\boxed{
\left[
(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)^n,
\mathcal G_n^{IID}
\right].
}
\]
It is merely a special case of the general statistical space:
\[
\left[
(\Omega^{(n)},\mathcal F^{(n)},P^{(n)}),
\mathcal G_n
\right].
\]
The difference is that we have now imposed two strong simplifying assumptions on the DGP:
\[
\boxed{
\text{absence of dependence}
\quad+\quad
\text{absence of heterogeneity}
}
\]
or, equivalently,
\[
\boxed{
\text{Independence}
\quad+\quad
\text{Identical Distribution}.
}
\]
IID is therefore an assumption about the DGP. It is not something that arises simply because we collect many observations.

title: The IID Case
section: 6. Why do we not yet have a random sample?
text:
6. Why do we not yet have a random sample?
So far, we have constructed a sequence of random trials:
\[
\boxed{
\mathcal G_n^{IID}
=
\{T_1,T_2,\ldots,T_n\}.
}
\]
Each trial produces an abstract outcome:
\[
T_i\longrightarrow\omega_i.
\]
We have not yet introduced random variables.
In the next step, we will build the bridge
\[
\boxed{
T_i
\longrightarrow
X_i
\longrightarrow
x_i
}
\]
where
\[
\begin{array}{rcl}
T_i &:& \text{trial }i,\\
X_i &:& \text{random variable associated with trial }i,\\
x_i &:& \text{actual observed value.}
\end{array}
\]
Only then will we be able to formally define
\[
\boxed{
X^{(n)}=(X_1,\ldots,X_n)
}
\]
as a sample.
And when \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) are IID,
\[
\boxed{
X^{(n)}_{IID}=(X_1,\ldots,X_n)
}
\]
we will have a random sample.
After realization,
\[
\boxed{
x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)
}
\]
will be the sample realization: the actual observed data.

title: Conditional Probability: Information, Updating Probabilities, and Bayes
text:
1. New information, a new question
In the chapter on IID, we used conditional probability to investigate whether knowing the result of one trial changes the probabilities associated with another.
Now let us study this idea in its own right:
We roll a fair die once. Before knowing the outcome, we ask what the probability is that it is even.
Let \(A=\{2,4,6\}\) (“even”) and \(B=\{4,5,6\}\) (“greater than 3”). Initially, \(P(A)=1/2\). We then receive the information that \(B\) has occurred: now, among \(4,5,6\), two outcomes are even. Thus,
\[
P(A)=\tfrac12,\qquad P(A\mid B)=\tfrac23.
\]
We have neither repeated the experiment nor changed the die. We have changed the information available about the outcome.

title: Conditional Probability: Information, Updating Probabilities, and Bayes
text:
2. The revised probability model
For events \(A,B\in\mathcal F\) with \(P(B)>0\), we define
\[
\boxed{P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}.}
\]
When we fix the event \(B\), the rule \(A\mapsto P(A\mid B)\) is a new probability law on the original events: the conditional probability law.
This is the meaning of the revised probability model emphasized by Tsitsiklis: now that we know that \(B\) has occurred, probabilities are calculated within \(B\) and appropriately normalized.
For example, \(P(B\mid B)=1\) and \(P(B^c\mid B)=0\).

title: Conditional Probability: Information, Updating Probabilities, and Bayes
section: 3. Probabilities as beliefs: what does this language mean?
text:
3. Probabilities as beliefs: what does this language mean?
Tsitsiklis also uses the language of probabilistic beliefs: a probability expresses the degree of plausibility we assign to an event within a model.
Receiving new information may lead to revised beliefs, that is, conditional probabilities that differ from the initial probabilities.
It is important to distinguish the language of information updating from a philosophical claim: the conditional probability formula holds regardless of whether we adopt a frequentist or a subjective interpretation of probability.

title: Conditional Probability: Information, Updating Probabilities, and Bayes
text:
4. The multiplication rule
The definition of conditioning implies:
\[
\boxed{P(A\cap B)=P(B)P(A\mid B).}
\]
If \(P(A)>0\), we can also write \(P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B\mid A)\). This rule is useful for reasoning about processes that unfold in stages.
Exercise 1. An urn contains 3 red balls and 2 blue balls. Two balls are drawn without replacement. What is the probability that both are red? Write your solution using conditional probabilities, without assuming independence.

title: Conditional Probability: Information, Updating Probabilities, and Bayes
section: 5. Total probability: different ways an event can occur
text:
5. Total probability: different ways an event can occur
If \(B_1,\ldots,B_k\) form a partition of the space, with \(P(B_j)>0\), then
\[
\boxed{P(A)=\sum_{j=1}^k P(A\mid B_j)P(B_j).}
\]
The law of total probability decomposes \(P(A)\) into mutually exclusive and exhaustive scenarios.
Exercise 2. A company ships 60% of its orders through carrier 1 and 40% through carrier 2. The probabilities of delay are 5% and 10%, respectively. What is the probability that a randomly selected order arrives late?

title: Conditional Probability: Information, Updating Probabilities, and Bayes
section: 6. Bayes: from observed information to possible scenarios
text:
6. Bayes: from observed information to possible scenarios
Suppose we know the probabilities of observing evidence \(A\) under each scenario \(B_j\). After observing \(A\), we want to determine the probability of each scenario.
Bayes’ theorem combines the multiplication rule with the law of total probability:
\[
\boxed{P(B_j\mid A)=\frac{P(A\mid B_j)P(B_j)}{\sum_{\ell=1}^kP(A\mid B_\ell)P(B_\ell)}},\qquad P(A)>0.
\]
In the language of belief updating, \(P(B_j)\) is the prior probability, and \(P(B_j\mid A)\) is the posterior probability. Bayes’ theorem does not assume that probabilities are subjective: it is an identity that holds within the probability model.
Exercise 3. Only 2% of manufactured items are defective. A test flags 90% of genuinely defective items and 5% of nondefective items as defective. If the test flags an item as defective, what is the probability that the item is actually defective? Explain why the answer is not 90%.

title: Conditional Probability: Information, Updating Probabilities, and Bayes
text:
7. Returning to independence
If \(A\) and \(B\) are independent and \(P(B)>0\), then \(P(A\mid B)=P(A)\): the information that \(B\) has occurred does not change the probability of \(A\).
But conditioning is not synonymous with dependence. Conditioning is the general operation of updating probabilities when an event is known to have occurred; independence is a special property of the joint probability law.
